title: Every Way to Change the Case

concept.title: A letter has two choices, a digit has one
body: For a string of letters and digits, you can change the case of each letter independently. A digit cannot change. So the recursion walks along the string: at a digit there is **one** way to continue, at a letter there are **two** (upper case or lower case). With `k` letters there are `2^k` results.

In the ASCII table every upper-case letter comes **before** every lower-case letter (`A` is 65, `a` is 97). Trying the upper-case option first therefore produces the results in ascending order without sorting.

statement: You are given a string of letters and digits. Print every string that can be made by changing the case of any letters (each letter can be upper or lower case; digits stay). Print them in ascending ASCII order (upper-case letters come before lower-case letters), one per line.
inputFormat: The only line has the string.
outputFormat: All different results in ascending order, one per line.
constraints: The string has only English letters and digits.

examples.note: The four results are A1B, A1b, a1B and a1b.

hints: At a digit there is one way to go on; at a letter there are two.
Try the upper-case form before the lower-case form to get ascending order.
Record the string when you have decided every position.

explanation: The recursion decides one position per call: a digit is copied, a letter is tried as upper case and then as lower case. Upper case sorts before lower case, so the results are ascending.
solution.complexity: Time O(2^k * n) for k letters, space O(n) besides the output.

code.python:
def variants(s, pos, current, out):
    if pos == len(s):
        out.append("".join(current))
        return
    ch = s[pos]
    options = [ch] if ch.isdigit() else [ch.upper(), ch.lower()]
    for option in options:
        current.append(option)
        variants(s, pos + 1, current, out)
        current.pop()

s = input().strip()

out = []
variants(s, 0, [], out)
print("\n".join(out))
